title: Vinography Unboxed: Week of 10/25/26
summary:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep, asking

The post Vinography Unboxed: Week of 10/25/26 appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep, asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

This past week included a zippy Picpoul Blanc from the San Simeon Estate brand run by the folks at Riboli Vineyards. Picpoul Blanc is fairly common in the southern Rhône Valley as well as in Southwest France, but you don’t see it much here in California. Taste this one, and you’ll wonder why that is. It’s a lot of fun to drink and lives up to the literal translation of “lip stinger” in a great way.

If most people haven’t tasted Picpoul Blanc, even fewer have probably tasted the grape known as La Crescent unless they have spent a lot of time in Midwest and Northeast winegrowing regions. Developed only in 2002 as a complex hybrid of a number of different grape varieties, it deals well with the chilly and wet conditions in New York’s Champlain Valley, where Rolling Hills Estate turns it into a pretty and drinkable white wine.

This week I’ve also got two new releases from Two Shepherds Winery to recommend. Their Grenache Blanc starts slightly funky, but ends with pleasing bright tropical melony flavors. Fans of chillable red wines will enjoy their crunchy Ancient Vine Cinsault made from the venerable Bechthold Vineyard in Lodi, whose vines just turned 140 years old this year.

Two more wines from Orr Wines in Washington State are also worth recommending this week. Admirably, the Royal Slope Red channels all proceeds to the Columbia Basin Health Association Othello Clinic, which provides healthcare to vineyard workers in the Columbia Valley. I really enjoyed Orr’s Grenache, which offered a nice balance between fruit and savory tones.

I’ve got three more wines to recommend from the Girard brand to recommend this week, including their Old Vine Zinfandel and their Napa Cabernet Sauvignon. The Aristry red blend is the classiest of the three, with its polished and refined fruit.

Finally, from Clos Pegase (which shares an owner with Girard), I can recommend their Napa Cabernet, as well as their flagship Hommage bottling. The latter is big, bold, and polished, but the folks looking for big reds from Napa won’t be disappointed with this robust mouthful.

Notes on all these wines below.

Tasting Notes

2025 San Simeon Winery “Reserve” Picpoul Blanc, Paso Robles, Central Coast, California
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of freshly chopped apples and a hint of lemon peel. In the mouth, bright apple and lemon pith flavors mix with a touch of vanilla and pink grapefruit. Bright, juicy acidity keeps the salivary glands working overtime. 13.7% alcohol. Certified sustainable. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $48

2025 Rolling Hills Estate Winery “Old Schoolhouse Vineyard” La Crescent, Champlain Valley, New York
Pale gold in color, this wine smells of candied lemon peel and yellow apples. In the mouth, the wine is bright and juicy with excellent acidity and flavors of Meyer and Eureka lemons, apples and pears, plus a hint of celery. La Crescent is a cold-hardy, hybrid grape developed in Minnesota that contains DNA from several grape species, including vinifera, labrusca, riparia, and rupestris. The wine also contains 15% Frontenac Gris. 12.7% alcohol. 70 cases made. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $45.

2022 Two Shepherds “A Tribute to Saralee – Cate’s Corner Vineyard” Grenache Blanc, Russian River Valley, Sonoma, California
A light hazy greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of struck match, yogurt, and melon. In the mouth, melon and Asian pear flavors mix with jackfruit and a bit of guava. Very good acidity and a faint chalky texture. Fermented with ambient yeasts and minimal sulfur additions. Aged in a combination of stainless steel and neutral oak. 12.9% alcohol. 75 cases made. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $28.

2023 Two Shepherds “Ancient Vine – Bechthold Vineyard” Cinsault, Lodi, California
Light ruby in color, this wine smells of cherries, boysenberries, and crushed stones. In the mouth, boysenberry and cherry notes mix with dried and freshly chopped herbs as leathery tannins coat the mouth and stiffen. Excellent acidity combined with the tannins gives this wine a crunchy quality. Floral notes linger in the finish. Fermented with ambient yeasts, 100% whole clusters, and minimal sulfur additions. Aged in neutral oak. Organically farmed vines planted in 1886. 12.6% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $30. click to buy.

2023 Orr Wines “Royal Slope Red” Red Blend, Royal Slope, Columbia Valley, Washington
Dark garnet in color, this wine smells of cherries and black plums. In the mouth, black plum, cola, cherry, and earth are wrapped in thick, fleecy tannins that coat the mouth and stiffen with time. Very good acidity. Muscular and perhaps better with some time in the bottle. 14.1% alcohol. All proceeds benefit the Columbia Basin Health Association Mobile Clinic for vineyard workers. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $27.

2024 Orr Wines Grenache, Columbia Valley, Washington
Light ruby in the glass with garnet highlights, this wine smells of strawberries, chopped herbs, and road dust. In the mouth, strawberry and chopped-herb flavors are wrapped in cottony tannins that stiffen with time. Excellent acidity makes for a juicy quality. A hint of something vegetal lingers in the finish. Very tasty. Fermented in open-top bins with punchdowns. Pressed to old oak barrels, then bottled unfiled and unfiltered. 14.42% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $30. click to buy.

2022 Girard Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherry, cola, and mocha. In the mouth, fleecy tannins surround flavors of sweet black cherry, cola, and blackberry. Oak lingers in the finish. Very good acidity. Aged 16 months in 45% new French oak. 14.5% alcohol. 7500 cases made. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $36. click to buy.

2022 Girard “Old Vine” Zinfandel, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark garnet in color, this wine smells of crushed blackberries and black licorice. In the mouth, blackberry and black licorice mix with raisins and prunes as fleecy tannins coat the mouth. There’s enough acidity here to keep things fresh, but this is a ripe, dark wine for sure. Notes of black pepper linger in the finish. 15% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $31. click to buy.

2022 Girard “Artistry” Red Blend, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherries, blueberries, and blackberries. In the mouth, blueberry and black cherry flavors are bright with juicy acidity and wrapped in a thick, fleecy blanket of tannins that remain supple throughout. Notes of blackberry linger with the black cherry in the finish. A ripe, big-shouldered wine. A blend of 76% Cabernet Sauvignon, 10% Malbec, 7% Merlot, 6% Petit Verdot, and 1% Cabernet Franc aged for 18 months in 45% new French oak. 14.5% alcohol. 1010 cases made. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $60. click to buy.

2022 Clos Pegase Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark garnet in color, this wine smells of black cherries, tobacco leaf, and cola. In the mouth, cherry, tobacco, cola, and cocoa powder flavors are wrapped in muscular, fleecy tannins that stiffen a bit with time. Decent acidity. Mocha notes of oak linger in the finish. Destemmed and half of the grapes crushed. Fermented with commercial yeasts after a 4-day cold soak. Twice-daily pumpovers. Aged 15 months in 45% new French oak. 14.9% alcohol. 1792 cases made. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $51. click to buy.

2023 Clos Pegase “Hommage” Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark, almost opaque garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherries, graphite, mocha, and blueberries. In the mouth, chocolatey flavors of black cherry, blueberry, and graphite mix with cassis and dried herbs. Fleecy tannins coat the mouth and stiffen with time, but very good acidity keeps the wine fresh. Very well balanced for its 15.5% alcohol, though there is a touch of warmth in the finish. A big, brawny, but polished wine for those who want massive Cabernets. Destemmed, cold-soaked for 4 days, and then fermented warm with twice-daily pumpovers. Aged 18 months in 50% new French oak. 15.5% alcohol. 120 cases made. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $111. click to buy.

title: Vinography Images: The Anomaly
summary:

The post Vinography Images: The Anomaly appeared first on Vinography.
content:
The word you’re likely to hear most often while visiting the Douro wine region is schist. There’s a lot of what the Portuguese call schist in the Douro (though in English we’d call most of it slate), and the product of this rocky terroir is undeniably fantastic. There are a couple of special places in the Douro, however, where the geology under the vines is something entirely different. And one part of the Quinta do Vale Meão is one of those places. On the northern part of the estate, close to the river, a huge bed of fine red sand underlies the vineyard and stands in stark contrast to the grey and green hills that surround it.

title: San Francisco’s Local-Wine Complex
summary:
San Francisco and its immediate surrounds have never been more packed with places where a thirsty wine lover can sit

The post San Francisco’s Local-Wine Complex appeared first on Vinography.
content:
San Francisco and its immediate surrounds have never been more packed with places where a thirsty wine lover can sit down to a great glass of wine. Almost 20 years ago, I started keeping track of local wine bars, of which there were only a handful. Since then, that number has exploded to more than 60, and there are roughly 4,000 restaurants now. And, as the lean years of the pandemic fade into the rear-view mirror, wine lists are again showing variety and heft.

Even so, San Francisco proves to be something of a conundrum for those who wish to drink local. In a region known for all but inventing the farm-to-table dining movement in the US, the locavore ethos has curiously never managed to pervade the wine-drinking culture.

Nearly every wine list in the city will have some California wine on it, but only a few venues seem dedicated to featuring local wine. Instead, most lists mirror the city’s famously cosmopolitan qualities, offering amazing things to drink from the world’s best- (and least-) known wine regions, with only a small percentage (usually 5–15% of the wines on offer) from California. These lists are a delight for both the curious and the discerning wine lover, but they ultimately come at the expense of showcasing and supporting California’s thousands of wineries.

The first part of my monthly column for Jancis Robinson’s website has been made free to read this month, so read the full article introduction here.

The article is followed by my list of the best places to drink California wine in San Francisco, which is only available to subscribers.

My monthly column at JancisRobinson.Com, is available only to subscribers of her website. If you’re not familiar with the site, I urge you to give it a try. It’s only $135 a year (25% off for the holidays!), and well worth the cost, especially considering you basically get free, searchable access to the Oxford Companion to Wine ($65) and maps from the World Atlas of Wine ($50) as part of the subscription costs. Click here to sign up.

title: S.O.R.B.E.T Wine Tasting: Nov 8, San Francisco
summary:
I don’t know about you, but I love me a good acronym. S.O.R.B.E.T stands for Sonoma Organic Regenerative Biodynamic Educational

The post S.O.R.B.E.T Wine Tasting: Nov 8, San Francisco appeared first on Vinography.
content:
I don’t know about you, but I love me a good acronym. S.O.R.B.E.T stands for Sonoma Organic Regenerative Biodynamic Educational Tasting, and it’s put on by a group of like-minded Sonoma winemakers and winegrowers who have gotten together to highlight their county’s progress towards more ecologically minded ways of farming and winemaking in an era where greenwashing is also on the rise. These are producers who are not just farming organically but are sequestering carbon, capturing runoff, preventing erosion, improving ecology, and supporting communities of people.

Organized by three school friends in the wine business—Morgan Twain-Peterson of Bedrock Wine Co., Katie Bundschu of Gundlach Bundschu, and Sam Coturri of Winery Sixteen600—this event brings together a group of extremely high-integrity wine producers for a walk-around tasting of some really excellent wine.

The list of producers pouring includes: Abbot’s Passage, Bedrock Vineyard, Bedrock Wine Co, Benziger Family Winery, Brown Estate, BUCKLIN, Canihan Family Winery, Dane Cellars, Donum Estate, Enterprise Vineyards, Fest Wine Co., Fresh Wine Co, Gloria Ferrer, Gundlach Bundschu, Hamel Family Wine, Hanzell, Hill of Tara Winery, Kamen Estate Wines, Kivelstadt Cellars, KORBIN KAMERON, Jambe de Bois, Las Vivas, Lasseter Family Winery, Laurel Glen Vineyard, Marioni Wine, Montecillo Vineyard, Once & Future Wine, Pangloss Cellars, Ram’s Gate Winery, Rossi Ranch, Stone Edge Farm Estate Vineyards & Winery, Tidings, Winery Sixteen 600

This will be a delicious way to spend an afternoon, I promise.

2026 Sonoma Organic Regenerative Biodynamic Educational Tasting
Sunday, November 8 – 1:00 PM to 4:00 PM
Fort Mason Center, Gallery 308
2 Marina Boulevard
San Francisco, CA 94123 (map)

Tickets to the event will run you $78.30, and should be purchased in advance online. My advice? Get a good night’s sleep, grab a big lunch ahead of time, and spit so you can try a lot of stuff and still keep your head.

title: Vinography Unboxed: Week of 10/18/26
summary:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep, asking

The post Vinography Unboxed: Week of 10/18/26 appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep, asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

This week included a new sparkling wine from the folks at Jackson Family Wines, who have been investing heavily in Oregon in recent years. This new project, Banke Wines, is named after the company’s CEO, Barbara Banke, who swears that she didn’t choose the name for this new line of sparkling wines. The Blanc de Blancs they sent me recently was impeccably made and offered a wonderfully brilliant lemony zing in the glass with just the right balance between fruity freshness and the patina you can get with long lees aging in the bottle. I highly recommend it.

Erica Orr worked as a lab tech at UCSF Hospital in San Francisco, but then a chance meeting with winemaker Aaron Pott at a bar in San Francisco led her down the rabbit hole of winemaking. A bunch of internships, a master’s degree, and years as a consulting enologist later, Erica is making her own wines in Washington State. Her old-vine Chenin Blanc and Salumeria Blend red wines are both very drinkable and tasty, not to mention affordable.

Girard Winery is a brand brought back to life in Napa. Originally a family-owned winery based in Oakville, the physical winery and brand were sold in 1996 to Leslie Rudd, who turned it into Rudd Estate. The Girard brand was purchased from Rudd by Pat Roney in 2000, who made wine under that name even as Roney combined it with Windsor Vineyards to create the company Vintage Wine Estates, which went on to acquire a number of other brands. VWE went bankrupt in 2024, and a number of its brands, including Girard and Clos Pegase, were purchased by Jay Adair, who has pulled them together under the banner of Adair Family Wines. I’m recommending three Girard wines this week: their bright Sauvignon Blanc and their rich and dark Charbono and Mixed Blacks red blend.

Hensel West is a new wine project by Will and Amanda Phelps. Will, of course, is the third generation of the Phelps Family making wine in Napa, after his pioneering grandfather Joseph Phelps established his namesake winery in 1973. To make their wines, Will and Amanda have hired winemaker Ashley Hepworth, who spent 15 years making the wines at Joseph Phelps. They sent through their inaugural bottlings of Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah, and a Bordeaux-style blend for me to try this week. They’re all solid, but the red blend is a standout, offering a refined texture and a nicely restrained expression of fruit. The winery is aiming for a luxury positioning, and all the wines are allocated straight out of the gate, apparently. But if you’re in the market for pricey Napa wines, this is one to keep an eye on.

Notes on all these below.

Tasting Notes

NV Banke “Blanc de Blancs” Chardonnay, Willamette Valley, Oregon
Pale gold in the glass with medium-fine bubbles, this wine smells of freshly cut apples, sea air, and lemon peel. In the mouth, a soft mousse delivers flavors of lemon peel, lemon oil, pomelo, and oyster shells as fantastic acidity makes the mouth water. There’s a hint of salinity here that adds to the overall very delicious package. A whisper of vanilla and crushed nuts lingers in the finish. Barrel-fermented. Spent 47 months on the lees in the bottle before disgorgement in August 2026. 6.5 g/L dosage. 12.5% alcohol. LIVE-certified sustainable. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $70.

2025 Orr “Old Vine” Chenin Blanc, Columbia Valley, Washington
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of pear and candied ginger. In the mouth, pear and ginger flavors mix with white flowers and a hint of citrus pith. There’s a faint lanolin note that also lingers in the finish. Decent acidity, but I would like more. Fermented with ambient yeasts in old oak barrels and steel drums. Bentonite-fined and sterile-filtered before bottling. 12% alcohol. 386 cases made. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $28. click to buy.

2025 Girard Sauvignon Blanc, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Palest gold in the glass, near colorless, this wine smells of green apples and passionfruit. In the mouth, green apple, passionfruit, and a hint of green bell pepper have a nice brightness thanks to decent acidity. Fermented with ambient yeasts in stainless steel. Malolactic inhibited. 14.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $21. click to buy.

2025 Hensel West “Riverbound Vineyard” Sauvignon Blanc, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Palest greenish-gold in the glass, this wine smells of white flowers, oak, and apples. In the mouth, bright, juicy acidity makes flavors of lemon pith, unripe apple, and crushed nuts quite mouthwatering. The oak is a definite presence here and has the effect of compressing the wine at this point in its evolution, giving an overall impression of narrowness. 14% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $65.

2024 Orr “Salumeria Blend” Red Blend, Columbia Valley, Washington
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of cherries, sour cherries, and a hint of cocoa powder. In the mouth, cherry, cocoa powder, sawdust, and a touch of dried herbs are wrapped in faint gauzy tannins. Decent acidity. A blend of 58% Sangiovese, 37% Cabernet Sauvignon, and 5% Merlot. Aged in old French oak for 10 months. Bottled unfined and unfiltered. 14.1% alcohol. 190 cases made. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $30. click to buy.

2022 Girard Charbono, Calistoga, Napa, California
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of blueberries, woodsmoke, espresso, and licorice. In the mouth, blueberries, licorice, and a smoky blackberry flavor are all wrapped in fine tannins. Decent acidity. Notes of oak and dark berries linger in the finish.13.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $75.

2022 Girard “Mixed Blacks” Red Blend, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of blackberries, earth, licorice, and espresso. In the mouth, sweet oak and espresso notes mix with blackberry and black cherry flavors as fleecy tannins coat the mouth. Heavily oak-inflected, but with enough acidity to keep things fresh. 14.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $70.

2024 Hensel West “Hyde Vineyard” Syrah, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of blueberries, black cherries, and licorice. In the mouth, black cherry and blueberry flavors are smooth and taut across the palate, with fine, powdery tannins and decent acidity. There’s a faint stoniness to the wine, but I would love some more acidity. 14.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $110.

2024 Hensel West “HWX” Red Blend, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in color, this wine smells of black cherry, tobacco, and espresso. In the mouth, fine-grained micro-fleece tannins surround a core of black cherry, blackberry, and espresso notes. Very good acidity. Hold for 3-7 years for best results. A blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, and Petit Verdot aged in 80% new French oak for 19 months.14% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $200.

title: California Cult Bubbles and More: The Latest from Ultramarine & Cruse Wine Co.
summary:
If there were a competition for California’s geekiest winemaker, I’m sure Michael Cruse would make the final round. His willingness

The post California Cult Bubbles and More: The Latest from Ultramarine & Cruse Wine Co. appeared first on Vinography.
content:
If there were a competition for California’s geekiest winemaker, I’m sure Michael Cruse would make the final round. His willingness to dive into the minutiae of (mostly sparkling) winemaking is unparalleled in my experience, something I’m reminded of when I show up to taste at his office, where a 4-foot-by-6-foot poster charting all the metabolic pathways known to science occupies almost the entirety of one wall. I’ll never forget the story he once told me of trying to culture his own yeast and making one of the biggest messes of his life.

The 46-year-old Cruse grew up in San Francisco and later moved to Petaluma. After studying molecular biology at UC Berkeley, Cruse worked in academic labs until he realized that he wasn’t feeding his soul. Inspired by a winemaker’s guest lecture during his college years, he tried his hand in the wine industry, first in enology labs and then in cellars, where he found his true calling.

After working his way up to Associate Winemaker at Merryvale’s Starmont winery in Napa, Cruse struck out on his own, opening a custom crush facility in Petaluma where he could make his own wines.

Along the way, he talked his way into getting some fruit from the legendary Heintz Vineyard on the Sonoma Coast and launched California’s first serious single-vineyard, extended-tirage sparkling wine brand known as Ultramarine. I’ve written in depth about the phenomenon that is Ultramarine before here on Vinography.

In addition to Ultramarine, which is made in such tiny quantities that it couldn’t really sustain a career or a household, Cruse makes a line of wines under the Cruse Wine Co. label that includes pét-nats, sparkling wines, and still red and white wines. The wines range from single-vineyard expressions to California-appellation blends of fruit from various sources. These wines have been designed from the start to be affordable and approachable.

“I was becoming ossified in Napa,” says Cruse about his career before deciding to start his own brand. “I was on the path to make $150 to $200 bottles, and it was bumming me out. With Cruse [Wine Co.], it was always going to be about making wines that people would drink.”

To that end, says Cruse, he hasn’t raised prices on his eponymous wines in 10 years. Ultramarine, too, remains relatively affordable to those on the mailing list, having risen from $45 to $80 or $95 a bottle over the course of 11 vintages. Of course, it trades at much higher prices on the secondary market thanks to its scarcity and high demand.

As top cuvées from some sparkling wine producers in California approach $200, Cruse’s wines, especially those made under the Cruse Wine Co. brand, begin to look like serious bargains. Affordability aside, Cruse has strong opinions about the correct approach to making sparkling wine in California.

“How should we be talking about California sparkling wine?” says Cruse. “This is one of the questions I have. It seems to me that instead of being afraid of sunshine, or overly indulgent, we can have density and weight that feel ripe but not overly fruity, which is where oxidation can come in.”

There are several points in the sparkling winemaking process where oxidation can play a positive role in shaping the character of the wine, but the three primary ones are how the juice is handled prior to and during the fermentation, how the still wine is aged prior to the secondary fermentation in the bottle, and the introduction of older, reserve wine into the overall blend.

Cruz presses slowly, allowing the juice longer contact with oxygen, and opting to ferment in barrels without adding sulfur dioxide continues that oxidative approach. The wines are then aged in barrels for a time with sulfur added to prevent malolactic fermentation, but the barrels allow further micro-oxygenation of the still wines. Finally, perpetual reserves (as Cruse uses with his “Tradition” sparkling wine) can hold a decade or more of older vintages and add further oxidative patina to balance out ripe fruit.

I do find Cruse’s sparkling wines, both those made under the Cruse label and Ultramarine, to be wonderfully balanced between fruit and more savory characteristics, though an extra edge and precision (perhaps thanks to the single-vineyard sourcing) give the Ultramarine wines a fineness that separates them from the Cruse bottlings.

Cruse does many things well when it comes to winemaking, but I particularly admire his attention to acidity. This goes especially for his still wines, which are often overlooked given his talents with bubbles. He’s particularly enamored with the Valdiguié grape variety, which has a long history in California. Long known in California as Napa Gamay, until ampelographers set the record straight, Valdiguié has many charms, not the least of which is a vibrant, juicy acidity accompanying a floral and berry flavor profile.

“It’s one of my favorite wines,” says Cruse, “but I can’t sell it to save my life.”

The Valdiguié and its sibling, the extremely quaffable Monkey Jacket, are, in my opinion, two of California’s better wine values, but they seem destined to remain in the shadow of the sparkling wines that have rightfully made Cruse so well known.

That’s something of a shame. For all his fascination with yeast metabolism and the esoterica of Champagne press cycles, Cruse is really after something pretty simple: wines people want to open on a weekday night. The science is just how he gets there. And since he’s taken care of all that geeky stuff for us, all we have to do is pull the cork.

Tasting Notes

2023 Cruse Wine Co. “Ricci Vineyard Pet Nat” Rosé of Saint Laurent, Los Carneros, Sonoma, California
Light coppery pink in the glass with extremely fine bubbles, this wine smells of peaches, orange creamsicle, and wet pavement. In the mouth, a soft mousse delivers flavors of bubble gum, stone fruit, plum, and citrus peel. Macerated for a few hours, pressed to bottling at 1-1.5 brix, with only the first gentle press fractions used (cuvée only, no taille). Spends 18 months in bottle and is sold undisgorged under a crown cap in pétillant naturel style. 11% alcohol. 4000 bottles made. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $36. click to buy.

2025 Cruse Wine Co. “Deming Pet Nat” Rosé of Valdiguié, Calistoga, Napa, California
Pale gold with a hint of peach and faint tiny bubbles, this wine smells of orange pith, unripe apricot, and a touch of pastry cream. In the mouth, a soft mousse delivers faintly sweet flavors of orange peel, white peach, berries, and a touch of dry herbs. Pretty and refreshing. Dry-farmed, organic 80+ year-old vines. Macerated for a few hours, pressed to bottling at 1-1.5 brix, with only the first gentle press fractions used (cuvée only, no taille). Spends 18 months in the bottle and is sold undisgorged under a crown cap in pétillant naturel style. 12% alcohol. 3500 bottles. Score: around 9. Cost: $35. click to buy.

NV Cruse Wine Co. “Tradition” Rosé Sparkling Wine, California
Light coppery peach in color with very fine bubbles, this wine smells of crabapples, warm wool, dried herbs, and dried flowers. In the mouth, a voluminous, silky mousse delivers flavors of orange peel, berries, a touch of crabapple, and a nice floral aromatic sweetness across the palate. Sophisticated and sensual, with great acidity, lift, and length on the palate. Extremely tasty. 95% Pinot Noir, 5% Chardonnay. Spends 36 months on the lees and receives 6 g/L dosage. All 2021 fruit. 12.5% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $60. click to buy.

NV Cruse Wine Co. “Tradition” Sparkling Wine, California
Light gold in the glass with a hint of bronze and fine bubbles, this wine smells of marzipan, biscotti, and roasted nuts. In the mouth, a silky, voluminous mousse delivers dried orange peel, roasted sesame and poppy seeds, savory dried herbs, and a touch of nougat. Long on the palate with a lovely energy and a mysterious aspect. Wonderfully delicious. A blend of 57% Pinot and 43% Chardonnay. Two-thirds of the juice comes from 2022 fruit, the remainder being a perpetual cuvée going back to 2015. Ages for 30 months on the lees in the bottle before being disgorged in January of 2026 with zero dosage.12.5% alcohol. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $50. click to buy.

2021 Cruse Wine Co. “Blanc de Noirs” Sparkling Wine, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Pale gold in the glass with very fine bubbles, this wine smells of crushed cashews, white flowers, and resinous herbs. In the mouth, salty crushed nuts, rosemary, bitter herbs, and wet chalkboard take on a chalky texture through the finish. Great acidity and lovely salinity. A radically distinctive and unusual wine. Some extra Pinot Noir fruit from Charlie Heintz became available, and the puncheons where the finished wine was aged were hard-bunged, taped, and not topped up, allowing some of them to form a blanket of flor yeast. The puncheons that didn’t get flor were moved into the rosé program. The wine was then aged for 30 months on the lees in bottle before disgorgement with zero dosage. 12.5% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $60.

2024 Cruse Wine Co. “Rorick Vineyard” Chardonnay, Sierra Foothills, California
Pale yellow-gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon blossom, candied lemon peel, and a hint of candle wax. In the mouth, silky flavors of lemon oil, lemon peel, and white flowers have a more delicate acidity and a faint stony minerality. Vines were planted in the late 1970s and are own-rooted, growing in mica-schist soils. Whole cluster pressed. 13.5% alcohol. 450 cases made. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $32. click to buy.

2023 Cruse Wine Co. “Rancho Chimiles” Valdiguié, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Medium purple in the glass, this wine smells of boysenberries and blueberries. In the mouth, stony and crunchy blueberry and boysenberry flavors are mixed with dried herbs and bright floral notes. Faint tannins have an amazing stony grip. Fantastic acidity and a sort-of-stony seamlessness that is quite alluring. Vines planted in the early 1970s. Fully destemmed and fermented in concrete, where it ages for 12 months before bottling. 12% alcohol. 275 cases made. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $33. click to buy.

2023 Cruse Wine Co. “Monkey Jacket” Red Blend, California
Medium garnet in the glass with purple highlights, this wine smells of boysenberries, blackberries, and dried herbs. In the mouth, boysenberries, licorice, charred vegetables, and dried herbs. Powdery tannins stiffen slightly, with excellent acidity keeping things fresh. Notes of purple SweetTarts linger in the finish. An equal blend of Valdiguié, Petite Sirah, Carignan, and Zinfandel, with a trace of Tannat, all fermented separately. The Valdiguie and Zinfandel are destemmed, the others with whole clusters. Blended early, and then aged for 12 months in a combination of 50% concrete and 50% neutral wood. 13% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $27. click to buy.

Note that the prices shown below are what the wines can be purchased for on the secondary market.

2021 Ultramarine “Michael Mara Blanc de Blancs” Sparkling Wine, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Pale yellow gold in the glass with fine bubbles, this wine smells of lemon pith, wet chalkboard, and a hint of toasted sesame. In the mouth, toasted sesame and crushed roasted nuts mix with white flowers and stony wet pavement, all borne on a silky, airy, voluminous mousse. Notes of dried herbs and citrus pith linger in the finish along with a hint of sourdough croutons. Long finish. Great poise. There’s a floral aspect that adds an extra allure to this stunning wine. 100% Chardonnay. The still wine spends about a year in 30% new large-format oak before secondary fermentation. Aged for 44 months on the lees in the bottle before disgorging in November 2025 with 2 g/L dosage. 12.5% alcohol. 1200 bottles made. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $190.

2021 Ultramarine “Charles Heintz Blanc de Blancs” Sparkling Wine, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Pale yellow gold in the glass with fine bubbles, this wine smells of salty struck match, charred lemon peel, and a hint of dried herbs. In the mouth, a mousse of moderate volume delivers salty flavors of lemon peel, toasted sourdough, a faint touch of green herbs, and gorgeous stony wet chalkboard minerality. Lemon peel and orange peel flavors linger in the finish with sea air and a touch of kelp. A stunning, electric wine that manages to be generous and electrically lean at the same time. 100% Chardonnay. The still wine spends about a year in 30% new large-format oak before secondary fermentation. Aged for 44 months on the lees in bottle before disgorging in November 2025 with 2 g/L dosage. 12.5% alcohol. 2000 bottles made. Score: between 9.5 and 10. Cost: $190. click to buy.

2021 Ultramarine “Charles Heintz Blanc de Noirs” Sparkling Wine, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Pale yellow gold in color with fine bubbles, this wine smells of wet chalkboard and cherries, white flowers, and acerola. In the mouth, a silky, voluminous mousse delivers flavors of acerola, cherry, saline citrus peel, gorgeous wet chalkboard, and a hint of tidepool. Tangy and mouthwatering, with a crazy salty candied citrus note that lingers in the finish for a long time. Simply gorgeous. 100% Pinot Noir. The still wine spends about a year in 30% new large-format oak before secondary fermentation. Aged for 44 months on the lees in bottle before disgorging in November 2025 with 2 g/L dosage. 12.5% alcohol. 1600 bottles made. Score: between 9.5 and 10. Cost: $172. click to buy.

2021 Ultramarine “Charles Heintz” Rosé Sparkling Wine, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Light coppery pink with a hint of orange and very fine bubbles, this wine smells of berries and a hint of hibiscus. In the mouth, a softer mousse delivers faint struck match and berry notes, saline with a lovely sea-air quality, and a touch of acerola and citrus peel lingering in the finish. A blend of 50% Pinot Noir, 50% Chardonnay, plus 5-8% still red wine for color. The still wine spends about a year in 30% new large-format oak before secondary fermentation. Aged for 44 months on the lees in bottle before disgorging in November 2025 with 6 g/L dosage. 12.5% alcohol. 4000 bottles made. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $180. click to buy.

2021 Ultramarine “Hirsch Vineyard” Sparkling Rosé of Pinot Noir, Fort Ross-Seaview, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Light coppery pink in the glass with fine bubbles, this wine smells of red apple skin, cranberries, citrus peel, and dried herbs. In the mouth, a softer, silky mousse delivers flavors of strawberry, biscuits, dried herbs, and a hint of crushed nuts. In the finish, there’s a dried herb quality that lingers for a long time. Fantastic. 100% Pinot Noir from Block 15 of Raschen Ridge at Hirsch Vineyards, saignéed after 12 hours of maceration. The still wine spends about a year in 30% new large-format oak before secondary fermentation. Aged for 44 months on the lees in bottle before disgorging in November 2025 with 6 g/L dosage. 12.5% alcohol. 4000 bottles made. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $160. click to buy.

Eric gets it exactly right.

TLDR? Wine is ok.

Savatiano and the Old Vines of Attica
How old is an old grape?

How El Niño Impacts a Wine Vintage
Jim Clarke looks into the possibilites

Shiraz and the wine industry Iran lost after 1979
A bit of history and a bit of speculation.

The Decisions That Will Define Wine in 2027
Hope is not a strategy.

Next Wave Awards Sommelier of the Year: Matt Turner
A worthy choice.

Why Jancis Robinson Remains Optimistic About Wine
Dave McIntyre talks with Jancis.

California loses nearly 10% of vineyard acreage in a year
Might not be enough?

Priorat’s Slate and the Return to Elegance: Jordi Fernández of Gratavinum
An interview.

Why Vesuvius was an opportunity for Roman wine investors
Don’t buy on the dip. Buy on the eruption.

Australia Joins the Global Vine Pull
$100m in government loans to rip out vineyards.

Move Over, Champagne: Ultra-Aged American Sparkling Wine Is Here
Pricey things these extended-tirage bottlings….

Behind the scenes at ASI Best Sommelier of the World 2026
Heck of a contest.

Arguably wine’s most labor-intensive process, this California winemaker has been at it for 25 years
Talk about a labor of love.

Samvel Machanyan of Alluria Wines on Natural Wine, Native Grapes and the Renaissance of Armenian Winemaking
In the shadow of Ararat.

EU wine industry welcomes rejection of tougher alcohol warnings
We should all welcome it too.

What happens when data centers come to wine country?
In a land with very little water, this is a serious question, asked by Sean Sullivan.
